## The idea

Equal clicks do not announce where a bar begins. A listener can count them in several plausible groups until a recurring difference gives one position more weight. An accent supplies that evidence without moving any event.

*Meter* is the recurring pattern of strong and weak beats through which a listener hears a bar. In a stream of eighth notes, accents every two subdivisions suggest quarter-note beats; accents every three suggest dotted-quarter beats. Six eighths therefore make a useful comparison. In 3/4, they fall into three groups of two. In 6/8, they fall into two groups of three. Both versions occupy three quarter-note beats, but their internal weight points to different meters.

The program keeps the six durations fixed and changes the amplitude cycle. Follow the strong clicks, then notice how the weaker clicks fit around them.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92

define :play_meter do |durations, accents, expected|
  raise "bar length mismatch" unless durations.sum == expected
  durations.each_with_index do |duration, index|
    sample :elec_tick, amp: accents[index % accents.length]
    sleep duration
  end
  sleep 1
end

eighths = [0.5] * 6
play_meter eighths, [1.2, 0.55], 3.0
play_meter eighths, [1.2, 0.55, 0.55], 3.0
play_meter eighths, [0.8], 3.0
```

Each pass uses the same sample, six eighth-note sleeps, and the same three-beat total. The first profile accents every other eighth and is designed to suggest three quarter-note groups. The second accents every third eighth and is designed to suggest two dotted-quarter groups. The final pass removes that amplitude evidence and leaves an even stream. Listening still determines how strongly each grouping comes across on the chosen sample and speakers.

## Change one thing

1. Reduce the strongest amplitude from `1.2` to `0.9`. As the difference between strong and weak events narrows, the meter becomes harder to infer even though the six onset positions remain fixed.

2. Restore the original and make the 6/8 profile `[1.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.9, 0.5, 0.5]`. The secondary accent at the fourth eighth marks the second half while keeping the first half strongest.

3. Restore the profiles and remove one eighth from the duration array. Keep the assertion. Read the error in the log and connect it to the half-beat missing from the promised three-beat bar.

## Why it works

The accent array is a repeating weight function. For each event, `index % accents.length` chooses a level from that cycle. A two-value array repeats strong–weak; a three-value array repeats strong–weak–weak. Applied to the same eighth-note stream, these cycles create different perceptual boundaries.

Validation solves another problem. `durations.sum == expected` checks that the bar occupies the promised amount of musical time. It cannot say how the listener will group that time. Both 3/4 and 6/8 equal three quarter-note beats here, so both pass the same assertion. Their accent profiles partition the span differently.

This separation is useful beyond the example. A bar can have the correct duration sum and an unconvincing meter if its emphasis points elsewhere. Conversely, a compelling accent pattern can be cut short by a missing event. The log catches the arithmetic fault; playback reveals the grouping.

Amplitude is one source of accent. A stronger attack attracts attention while leaving pitch, timbre, and duration unchanged, which makes it well suited to this comparison. Music can also create weight through a lower pitch, a different drum, a longer note, or a change in harmony. Those cues may reinforce one another, but they also add colour that makes the underlying pattern harder to isolate.

The unaccented pass deserves attention because it shows that meter is not printed into equal subdivisions. You may continue hearing the previous grouping from memory, or impose another one. Replay the three profiles in a different order and notice how context affects the neutral stream.

Lesson 14 adds rests and sustained events while keeping duration arithmetic intact. A bar does not cease to occupy time because one position has no attack, and a note can cross a boundary without striking it again.

## Take it further

Create one six-eighth duration array and three named accent profiles: 3/4, 6/8, and an even control. Select among them by editing one symbol. All three should pass one assertion that requires a total of three quarter-note beats.

Audition the profiles in Sonic Pi 5 without changing the sample or tempo. Mark the accent position that most clearly separates three groups of two from two groups of three. Then reduce that accent and listen again. The comparison should demonstrate both layers of the representation: a shared numerical span and different audible groupings.
